title: Starling murmurations
hook: Thousands of starlings turn as one, and no bird is in charge.
peek: On winter evenings, huge flocks of starlings pour across the sky in shapes that fold and ripple like smoke. There is no leader. Each bird watches only a handful of neighbours, and the whole cloud emerges from that.
lede: On autumn and winter evenings, starlings gather before roosting and fly in vast, shifting clouds called murmurations. Flocks can number in the tens or hundreds of thousands, and the shape ripples and folds as if one mind were steering it. There is no leader. Research suggests each bird is mostly tracking a few of its nearest neighbours.

bullets.text: A 2008 study in Rome filmed flocks in 3D and found that each starling responds to about six or seven nearby birds, whatever the distance between them. That keeps the flock together even as it stretches and thins.

In 1986, a computer graphics researcher showed that three simple rules, keep apart, match heading, stay close, were enough to make simulated birds flock convincingly. Versions of his method are now used for crowds and swarms in films.
Like the spirals in a sunflower head, a murmuration is order that nobody plans. Small local rules, repeated many times, produce a large shape that looks deliberate.
The leading idea is that the swirling makes it hard for a falcon or hawk to pick out a single bird. Murmurations often grow more dramatic when a predator is nearby.
Starlings are skilled mimics that can copy other birds, phones and car alarms. Mozart kept a pet starling in the 1780s and noted that it could sing a phrase from one of his piano concertos.
